steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on reasoning about unintentional activities in videos with large multimodal models, where hallucinations are the main obstacle. Motivate the task, explain what goes wrong with existing prompting, introduce our prompting approach, mention the datasets we test on, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Understanding human activities in videos; unintentional activities and why reasoning matters
2. Multimodal foundation models and the failure of existing prompting
3. Our approach: Dream of Thought prompting
4. Datasets and evaluation
5. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- automatic understanding of human activities in videos: challenging, real-world applications (healthcare, security, robotics, elderly assistance)
- impressive progress on intentional activities in past few years
- humans make mistakes; activities can be unintentional
- recognizing unintentional activities important, but also understanding reasoning behind them -> correcting mistakes, damage control
- focus: reasoning behind unintentional activities in videos

2. LMMs and prompting
- multimodal foundation models: strong across tasks, zero-shot generalization
- study reasoning of existing Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) via prompting, intentionality as actions transition to unintentional states
- conventional prompting: hallucinations, poor reasoning about transition
- even when transition identified -> generic reasons, visual context underused
- chain of thoughts: specific reasons, but still hallucinates

3. Our approach
- multi-step solution to mitigate hallucinations
- observations: 1) multiple hallucinations, some responses correct; 2) multiple-choice questions guide model to right answer
- Dream of Thought (DoT) prompting: hallucinations presented as multiple choices, model navigates to correct reasoning

4. Datasets
- OOPs: unintentional activities in daily life; UCF-Crimes: anomalous activities
- DoT beats simple prompting and chain of thoughts

5. Contributions
- novel problem: reasoning about transition from intentional to unintentional
- study of LMMs/prompting + DoT mechanism outperforming existing methods
- three evaluation protocols rm_{MCQ},rm_{LLM}, and rm_{FIB} for response matching (rm)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Automatically understanding human activities in videos is a challenging problem, and it has a lot of real-world applications in domains like healthcare, security, robotics, and elderly assistance. In the past few years there has been impressive progress in recognizing intentional human activities in videos. But human beings are prone to making mistakes, and in real-world scenarios activities can be unintentional. Recognizing unintentional activities is important, but it is also important to understand the reasoning behind why they happen. This can be useful for correcting mistakes and for damage control. Because of this, in this work we focus on finding the reasoning behind unintentional activities in videos. Multimodal foundation models that were developed recently have shown impressive capabilities on a range of tasks and generalize strongly in zero-shot scenarios. We first study the reasoning abilities of existing Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), using prompting to determine the intentionality of actions as we transition to unintentional states. Our analysis shows that conventional prompting techniques suffer from hallucinations and do not do well at reasoning about the transition into unintentional activities. We also noticed that even when the model can identify that the transition from intentional to unintentional has happened, it often gives very generic reasons and does not use the visual context fully. Chain of thoughts prompting gives a framework for getting specific reasons and not just generic ones, but it also suffers from hallucinations when trying to reason over unintentional activities.

Our approach
- multi-step solution to reduce hallucinations, improve reasoning
- observations: 1) let model hallucinate multiple times -> some responses correct; 2) multiple-choice questions guide model to right answer
- Dream of Thought (DoT) style prompting: hallucinations presented back as multiple choices, model navigates to correct reasoning

Datasets
- OOPs (unintentional activities in daily life), UCF-Crimes (anomalous activities)
- DoT more effective than simple and chain of thoughts prompting

Contributions
- new problem: reasoning about transition from intentional to unintentional
- study of LMMs + prompting; DoT mechanism outperforms existing methods
- three protocols rm_{MCQ},rm_{LLM}, and rm_{FIB} for response matching (rm)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Automatically understanding human activities in videos is a challenging problem, and it has a lot of real-world applications in domains like healthcare, security, robotics, and elderly assistance. In the past few years there has been impressive progress in recognizing intentional human activities in videos. But human beings are prone to making mistakes, and in real-world scenarios activities can be unintentional. Recognizing unintentional activities is important, but it is also important to understand the reasoning behind why they happen. This can be useful for correcting mistakes and for damage control. Because of this, in this work we focus on finding the reasoning behind unintentional activities in videos. Multimodal foundation models that were developed recently have shown impressive capabilities on a range of tasks and generalize strongly in zero-shot scenarios. We first study the reasoning abilities of existing Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), using prompting to determine the intentionality of actions as we transition to unintentional states. Our analysis shows that conventional prompting techniques suffer from hallucinations and do not do well at reasoning about the transition into unintentional activities. We also noticed that even when the model can identify that the transition from intentional to unintentional has happened, it often gives very generic reasons and does not use the visual context fully. Chain of thoughts prompting gives a framework for getting specific reasons and not just generic ones, but it also suffers from hallucinations when trying to reason over unintentional activities. To reduce the effect of hallucinations and improve reasoning over unintentional activities, we propose a multi-step solution. It relies on two key observations: 1) if we let a model hallucinate multiple times, some of the responses might be correct, and 2) multiple-choice questions help guide the model to the right answer. Building on these observations, we propose a new approach called Dream of Thought (DoT) style prompting. We take the model's hallucinations and present them to the model as multiple choices, and the model navigates through these choices and gives the correct reasoning.

We experiment with two datasets, OOPs and UCF-Crimes. OOPs focuses on unintentional activities in daily life and UCF-Crimes focuses on anomalous activities. With extensive evaluations we show that DoT prompting is more effective than simple prompting and chain of thoughts prompting. Our contributions in this work are:

- We present a new problem that is about reasoning on how an activity transitions from intentional to unintentional.

- We study how capable existing LMMs and prompting techniques are for this task, and we also give a new Dream of Thoughts (DoT) reasoning-based mechanism that outperforms existing methods.

- We give three evaluation protocols, rm_{MCQ},rm_{LLM}, and rm_{FIB}, for response matching (rm), which quantify how well models can reason for this task.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Automatic understanding of human activities in videos is a challenging problem with many real-world applications in domains such as healthcare, security, robotics, and elderly assistance. In the past few years, we have seen impressive progress in recognizing intentional human activities in videos [1]. However, human beings are prone to making mistakes, and activities can be unintentional in real-world scenarios. Recognizing unintentional activities is important [2], but it is also important to understand the reasoning behind their occurrence, which can be useful for correcting mistakes and for damage control. Motivated by this, in this work we focus on finding the reasoning behind unintentional activities in videos. Recently developed multimodal foundation models have shown impressive capabilities across a range of tasks, with strong generalization in zero-shot scenarios [3,4,5,6,7,8,9]. We first study the reasoning abilities of existing Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) using prompting to determine the intentionality of actions as we transition to unintentional states. Our analysis reveals that conventional prompting techniques suffer from hallucinations and do not perform well in reasoning about the transition into unintentional activities. We also noticed that even when the model is able to identify that the transition from intentional to unintentional has occurred, it frequently provides very generic reasons without fully using the visual context. Although chain of thoughts [10] prompting provides a framework to obtain specific rather than generic reasons, it also suffers from hallucinations when reasoning over unintentional activities. To mitigate the effect of hallucinations and improve reasoning over unintentional activities, we propose a multi-step solution, which relies on two key observations: 1) if we let a model hallucinate multiple times, some of the responses might be correct, and 2) multiple-choice questions help guide the model to the right answer. Building upon these observations, we propose a novel approach termed Dream of Thought (DoT) style prompting: we present the model's hallucinations to it as multiple choices and let the model navigate through these choices to provide correct reasoning.

We experiment with two different datasets, OOPs [2] and UCF-Crimes [11]; OOPs focuses on unintentional activities in daily life, while UCF-Crimes focuses on anomalous activities. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of DoT prompting over simple prompting and chain of thoughts prompting. We make the following contributions in this work:

- We present a novel problem focusing on reasoning about the transition of an activity from intentional to unintentional.

- We study the capability of existing LMMs and prompting techniques for this task, and provide a novel Dream of Thoughts (DoT) reasoning-based mechanism that outperforms existing methods.

- We provide three evaluation protocols, rm_{MCQ},rm_{LLM}, and rm_{FIB}, for response matching (rm), which quantify the reasoning capability of models for this task.
